cor-tr-classical.title: The classical transformations
cor-tr-classical.html:
1. Counts. If Y∼Poisson(μ), then 2(Y−μ)→N(0,1) as μ→∞.

  2. Proportions. If S∼Binomial(m,p) with 0<p<1 fixed and p^=S/m, then 2m{arcsin⁡p^−arcsin⁡p}→N(0,1) as m→∞.

  3. Constant coefficient of variation. If Y=μU for a positive random variable U whose distribution does not depend on μ, then Var(log⁡Y)=Var(log⁡U) exactly, for every μ, whenever it is finite.

  4. Power variance functions. If v(μ)=μ2a on (0,∞), then @eq-tr-stabilizing-integral gives μ1−a/(1−a) for a≠1 and log⁡μ for a=1. Up to an affine change this is the Box–Cox transformation with λ=1−a.

def-tr-box-cox.title: The Box–Cox family
def-tr-box-cox.html:
For y>0 and λ∈R, the Box–Cox transformation of y is y(λ)={yλ−1λ,λ≠0,log⁡y,λ=0.{#eq-tr-box-cox}

For a sample y1,…,yn>0 with geometric mean y˙=exp⁡(n−1∑ilog⁡yi), the normalized transformation is zi(λ)=yi(λ)/y˙λ−1, and z(λ)=(z1(λ),…,zn(λ))⊤.

eq-tr-box-cox.html: y(λ)={yλ−1λ,λ≠0,log⁡y,λ=0.

eq-tr-box-cox-loglik.html: 𝛃𝛃ℓ(β,σ2,λ)=−n2log⁡(2πσ2)−‖y(λ)−Xβ‖22σ2+(λ−1)∑i=1nlog⁡yi;

eq-tr-box-tidwell.html: 𝛃E(Y)=X2β2+β1x(α),x(α)=(x1(α),…,xn(α))⊤,

eq-tr-constructed.html: w(λ0)=∂z(λ)∂λ|λ=λ0,

eq-tr-cpr-mean.html: 𝛆E(ε^+β^1x1)=g−M2(g−bx1),b=E(β^1)=x~1⊤g‖x~1‖2.

eq-tr-elasticity.html: ∂m∂x1=β1x1α−1m1−λ,x1m∂m∂x1=β1x1αm−λ.

eq-tr-lr-interval.html: {λ0: nlog⁡SSEz(λ0)SSEz(λ^)≤χ1,α2},

eq-tr-mean-variance.html: Var(θ^)=σ2h0+σ42(n−r).

eq-tr-multiplicative.html: 𝛃Yi=exp⁡(x(i)⊤β)Ui,i=1,…,n,

eq-tr-power-constructed.html: w={(xiα0log⁡xi/α0)i=1n,α0≠0,(12(log⁡xi)2)i=1n,α0=0.

eq-tr-stabilizing-integral.html: g(μ)=∫μdtv(t).

eq-tr-transformed-model.html: 𝛃g(Yi)=x(i)⊤β+εi,i=1,…,n,

exm-tr-cpr-simulated.title: When the plot misleads
exm-tr-cpr-simulated.html: The script simulates 120 cases with E(Y)=3log⁡x1+x2, x1 uniform on [1,10], and measures how much of the curvature of g the expected plot keeps (the coefficient of the nonlinear part of g in that of @eq-tr-cpr-mean; 1 is faithful). In panel (a) of Figure 22.3.1, x2 is linear in x1 plus noise, with correlation 0.95, and the plot keeps 0.99. In panel (b), x2 is a noisy square root of x1, with correlation 0.99; it resembles the logarithm and takes over much of the curvature, and the plot keeps only 0.45, its slope even changing sign. The augmented plot, panel (c), restores 0.88.

exm-tr-engel-back.title: Engel’s data on the original scale
exm-tr-engel-back.title_html: Engel’s data on the original scale
exm-tr-engel-back.html:
With the log–log fit of @exm-tr-engel-scales, Figure 22.5.1 shows the data on the original scale with the fitted median curve, the smearing estimate of the mean and a 95% prediction band. For a household with income 500 the estimated median food expenditure is 352.2, with 95% confidence interval [342.2, 362.5], and a 95% prediction interval for a single household (@thm-ci-prediction-interval and @prp-tr-back-intervals(a)) is [269, 462]. At income 2000 the median is 1153.7, with interval [1111.7, 1197.3], and the prediction interval is [879, 1514]. A fraction 0.455 of the households lie below the fitted median curve.

The log-scale residual variance s2=0.01871 is small, and so is the retransformation bias: the smearing factor is 1.0091 and exp⁡(s2/2) is 1.0094. The estimated mean at income 2000 is 1164.2 by smearing and 1164.5 under normality, about one percent above the median. The approximate 95% interval for the mean from @eq-tr-mean-variance is [1122.4, 1208.3] at income 2000 and [345.4, 365.9] at income 500.

exm-tr-engel-box-cox.title: Box–Cox for Engel’s data
exm-tr-engel-box-cox.html:
First let transformed food expenditure be linear in income. The profile log-likelihood, panel (a) of Figure 22.2.1, peaks at λ^=0.63, and the 95% interval given by @eq-tr-lr-interval is [0.45, 0.80]. Both the raw scale and the logarithm are rejected: the likelihood ratio statistics are 18.8 for λ=1 and 37.2 for λ=0, against the critical value 3.84.

Now let food expenditure be linear in log income. The profile, panel (b), peaks at λ^=0.025, with interval [−0.117, 0.162]. The logarithm is well inside, with statistic 0.12, while the square root (46.6) and the raw scale (181.4) are firmly rejected. With log income as the regressor, the normalized residual standard deviation is 78.6 on the log scale and 115.6 on the raw scale, both in the currency of the survey (the geometric mean of food expenditure is 574.4).

The answers differ because a response transformation is chosen to make a particular mean function linear. Section 22.3 estimates the two powers together.

exm-tr-engel-box-tidwell.title: Transforming income
exm-tr-engel-box-tidwell.html:
With log⁡(food) as the response and income(α) as the regressor, starting from α0=1, the Box–Tidwell iteration gives −0.053 after one step and −0.182 after two, where it stays. The direct minimization agrees: α^=−0.182, with 95% likelihood ratio interval [−0.334, −0.036]. The constructed-variable t statistic is −16.58 at α0=1, so untransformed income is decisively rejected, and −2.47 at α0=0, beyond the critical value 1.97, so the logarithm is rejected at the 5% level as well. As a check on part (a), 4000 data sets simulated from the log–log fit give a rejection rate of 0.047 for this test.

The rejection rests largely on one household. The richest, with income 4958 and food expenditure 1827, sits far to the right in panel (c) of Figure 22.1.1, below the line. Without it, α^=−0.119, and the likelihood ratio statistic for α=0 falls from 5.98 to 1.77. A negative power says food expenditure flattens among the richest households, where the data are few; Cook’s distance (@def-res-cooks) pursues this.

exm-tr-engel-constructed.title: The constructed variable for Engel’s data
exm-tr-engel-constructed.title_html: The constructed variable for Engel’s data
exm-tr-engel-constructed.html:
In the model with log income, the constructed variable for λ0=1 has coefficient γ^=0.831 and t=17.96: overwhelming evidence against the raw scale. The one-step estimate 1−0.831=0.169 is far from λ^=0.025, as expected from so far away. For λ0=0 the coefficient is −0.031 with t=−0.38.

In 4000 data sets simulated from the fitted log–log model, with normal errors and Engel’s incomes (so λ=0 is true), the 95% likelihood ratio interval covers 0 in a fraction 0.945, close to nominal, while the nominal 5% constructed-variable test rejects in a fraction 0.075. The constructed variable is a diagnostic; the likelihood interval is for inference.

Deleting one household at a time, the largest change moves λ^ from 0.025 to 0.081, when the household with income 2823 and food expenditure 2033, the largest in the survey, is removed. It lies well above the line in panels (a) and (c) of Figure 22.1.1, at a point of high leverage (the leverage of Engel’s households is examined in Section 20.2). The logarithm stays inside the interval whichever household is removed. For a fixed scale Chapter 20 gives deletion formulas (@thm-res-deletion, and @prp-cmp-loo for their computation); for λ^ the refits are cheap enough to do directly.

exm-tr-engel-joint.title: Two powers for Engel’s data
exm-tr-engel-joint.html:
Figure 22.3.2 shows the joint profile. The maximum is at (λ^,α^)=(−0.25, −0.39). The raw scale (1,1) has likelihood ratio statistic 186.5, and the best pair with untransformed income, (0.63,1) from @exm-tr-engel-box-cox, has 167.8: whatever is done to the response, income needs transforming. The log–log pair (0,0) has statistic 11.2, outside the 95% region, whose cut-off is 5.99 for two parameters. Without the richest household the statistic falls to 6.55, still outside.

The region is a long tilted ellipse, since a lower response power can be partly compensated by a lower income power (@exr-tr-power-law-ridge). The log–log model lies outside the region (11.2 against 5.99), largely because of the richest household. It is still the natural working choice for interpretation, since its slope is an elasticity, with the caveat that the data reject a constant elasticity and that it may fall among the richest households (@prp-tr-elasticity).

exm-tr-engel-scales.title: Food expenditure on the raw and the log scale
exm-tr-engel-scales.title_html: Food expenditure on the raw and the log scale
exm-tr-engel-scales.html:
Engel’s survey of 235 Belgian households (@exm-proj-engel) records annual income, from 377 to 4958 in the survey’s currency, and expenditure on food. The least squares line on the raw scale has slope 0.4852, and panel (b) of Figure 22.1.1 shows a fan: the residual standard deviation among the richest third of households is 3.55 times that among the poorest third. The residuals have excess kurtosis 9.64 (zero for a normal distribution), largely a by-product of the fan, since a mixture of normals with different spreads has heavy tails.

On the log–log scale both defects nearly disappear. The spread ratio falls to 1.32, the excess kurtosis to −0.02, and the residual plot, panel (d), shows a horizontal band. The slope is 0.8559 with standard error 0.0203 and 95% interval [0.816, 0.896]. It is an elasticity (Section 5.7): households with 1 percent more income spend about 0.86 percent more on food. That the interval lies below one is Engel’s law, that the share of the budget spent on food falls as income rises.

exm-tr-skewed-errors.title: Skewed errors
exm-tr-skewed-errors.html: The script simulates the log-linear model log⁡Y=1+0.5x+ε with n=100 equally spaced values of x in [0,2] and right-skewed errors ε=0.6(E−1), E exponential with mean 1. The errors have mean 0 and variance 0.36. The true factor is Eeε=e−0.6/0.4, about 1.372, while the normal-theory factor exp⁡(0.36/2) is about 1.197. At x0=1, averaged over 4000 samples, the ratio of the estimate to the true mean is 0.730 for the naive 𝛃exp⁡(x0⊤β^), 0.877 for the normal-theory correction and 0.986 for the smearing estimate. Its remaining bias of about one percent reflects that residuals vary slightly less than errors.

exr-tr-additive-log.title: B1
exr-tr-additive-log.html: Let Y=μ+ε with μ>0, Eε=0, Varε=σ2 and σ/μ small. Use log⁡(1+u)=u−u2/2+O(u3) to show that, to the leading order, Elog⁡Y≈log⁡μ−σ2/(2μ2) and Varlog⁡Y≈σ2/μ2. Conclude that when errors are additive with constant variance, the log scale is heteroscedastic, with the variance falling as the mean rises, and its mean is not exactly log⁡μ.

exr-tr-anscombe.title: C1
exr-tr-anscombe.html: Let Y∼Poisson(μ) and c≥0. Expand Y+c=μ(1+u)1/2 with u=(Y−μ+c)/μ to third order in u, use the Poisson central moments E(Y−μ)2=μ, E(Y−μ)3=μ, E(Y−μ)4=3μ2+μ, and show formally that VarY+c=14+(3−8c)/(32μ)+O(μ−2). (The expansion is formal: making the remainder rigorous needs a bound on the tail of Y.)

exr-tr-asymmetric-pi.title: A2
exr-tr-asymmetric-pi.html: Explain why the prediction interval of @exm-tr-engel-back, obtained from @thm-ci-prediction-interval, is longer above the median than below it, and why its coverage is nevertheless exactly 95% under the normal model on the log scale.

exr-tr-augmented.title: B3
exr-tr-augmented.html: Let X=[x1,x12,X2], with 1∈C(X2) and full column rank, and let 𝛃E(Y)=g+X2β2. Show that the augmented partial residuals 𝛆ε^+β^1x1+β^11x12 have expectation g−M2(g−b1x1−b11x12), where (b1,b11) are the expectations of (β^1,β^11). Conclude that the plot is exact, up to a vertical shift, when g is a quadratic.

exr-tr-box-cox-influence.title: C2
exr-tr-box-cox-influence.html: Let λ^ be an interior maximizer of ℓp, and write 𝛆s(λ)=ε^(λ)⊤w(λ), which is zero at λ^ by @prp-tr-constructed. Suppose case i is deleted. Show, by one Newton step for the equation s=0, that the change in λ^ is approximately proportional to the contribution ε^(i)w~(i) of that case, where both factors are computed with the case deleted. Which cases does this predict to be influential for λ^, and how does leverage in the regression of w on X enter?

exr-tr-box-cox-values.title: A1
exr-tr-box-cox-values.html: Compute 4(λ) for λ=−1,0,12,1,2. Check that the values increase with λ, and explain, using the definition, why y(λ) is increasing in λ for every fixed y>0.

exr-tr-constructed-zero.title: B1
exr-tr-constructed-zero.html: Derive the constructed variable at λ0=0. Write z(λ)=f(λ)y˙1−λ with f(λ)=(yλ−1)/λ, expand f(λ)=log⁡y+12λ(log⁡y)2+O(λ2), and show that ∂z(λ)/∂λ at 0 is 12y˙{log⁡(y/y˙)}2−12y˙(log⁡y˙)2.

exr-tr-cpr-quadratic.title: B4
exr-tr-cpr-quadratic.html:
In the setting of @prp-tr-cpr, let X2=[1,q] with qi=xi12, so the second regressor is an exact quadratic in the first, and write 𝛃β2=(β20,δ)⊤.

  1. If g(x)=cx2, show that b=0 and that the expected partial residuals are 0: the plot is flat, although E(Y) curves in x1 when δ≠−c.

  2. If g(x)=cx, show that the plot is exact.

  3. Explain why no plot against x1 can tell which of the two regressors carries the curvature in (a).

exr-tr-cubic-variance.title: A1
exr-tr-cubic-variance.html: Find the variance-stabilizing transformation for v(μ)=μ3, the variance function of the inverse Gaussian distribution. Which Box–Cox power is it?

exr-tr-delta-check.title: B3
exr-tr-delta-check.html: For Engel’s data at income 500, s2=0.01871, h0=0.01147 and n−r=233. Evaluate the two terms of @eq-tr-mean-variance with σ2 replaced by s2, and check the standard error 0.0147 used for the interval [345.4, 365.9]. Which term dominates, and why?

exr-tr-elasticity-reading.title: A1
exr-tr-elasticity-reading.html: In the log–log fit of @exm-tr-engel-scales the slope is 0.8559. By what factor does the median food expenditure differ between two households whose incomes differ by 10 percent? By what factor between households whose incomes differ by a factor of two? Why is the answer the same for the median, the geometric mean and, under @eq-tr-multiplicative, the mean?

exr-tr-empirical-logit.title: B2
exr-tr-empirical-logit.html: Let S∼Binomial(m,p) with 0<p<1. Show by the delta method that m{logit(S/m)−logitp}→N(0,1/{p(1−p)}), where logitp=log⁡{p/(1−p)}. For independent groups i=1,…,k with Si∼Binomial(mi,pi) and 𝛃logitpi=x(i)⊤β, write down the weighted least squares estimate of 𝛃β from the empirical logits, and its approximate covariance matrix.

exr-tr-exponential-mean.title: A2
exr-tr-exponential-mean.html: Let Tm be the mean of m independent exponential waiting times with mean θ>0. Find the variance-stabilizing transformation. Use @thm-tr-variance-stabilizing(b) to show that the square root, although it stabilizes Poisson counts, does not stabilize Tm, and find the limiting variance of m(Tm−θ).

exr-tr-hetero-smearing.title: C2
exr-tr-hetero-smearing.html: Suppose that on the log scale εi∼N(0,σ2(x(i))), independent, with the variance depending on the regressors. Show that 𝛃E(Y∣x0)=exp⁡{x0⊤β+σ2(x0)/2}, and that, when the leverages tend to zero and the average n−1∑iexp⁡{σ2(x(i))/2} converges to a limit c¯, the smearing factor tends to c¯. For which x0 does the smearing estimate overestimate the mean, and for which does it underestimate it?

exr-tr-lr-difference.title: B2
exr-tr-lr-difference.html: In @exm-tr-engel-box-cox, with log income as regressor, the normalized residual standard deviations are 78.6 at λ=0 and 115.6 at λ=1. Show from @eq-tr-profile that the difference between the likelihood ratio statistics at λ=1 and λ=0 is 2nlog⁡{sz(1)/sz(0)}, and check it against the values 181.4 and 0.12 of the example.

exr-tr-median-bias.title: B1
exr-tr-median-bias.html: Under normal errors on the log scale, show that 𝛃𝛃Eexp⁡(x0⊤β^)=exp⁡(x0⊤β+σ2h0/2), so the naive median estimate is biased upwards by a factor that tends to one as h0→0. Suggest an approximately mean-unbiased alternative, and explain why 𝛃exp⁡(x0⊤β^) is exactly median-unbiased.

exr-tr-negative-binomial.title: B1
exr-tr-negative-binomial.html: Negative binomial counts have v(μ)=μ+μ2/κ for a shape parameter κ>0. Show that @eq-tr-stabilizing-integral gives g(μ)=2κsinh−1⁡μ/κ. Show that g behaves like 2μ for μ≪κ and like κlog⁡μ plus a constant for μ≫κ, and interpret.

exr-tr-no-effect.title: C1
exr-tr-no-effect.html: Suppose that the conditional distribution of Y given (x1,…,xk) does not depend on x1. Show that the same holds for g(Y) for every strictly increasing g, so the hypothesis that x1 has no effect is the same hypothesis on every scale. Why does the converse direction, from a zero coefficient on one scale to a zero coefficient on another, fail when the conditional distribution does depend on x1? Give an example with two groups whose medians are equal but whose means are not.

exr-tr-no-slope.title: C1
exr-tr-no-slope.html: Suppose β1=0 in @eq-tr-box-tidwell. Show that the model does not depend on α, so α is not identified. Show that the test of @thm-tr-box-tidwell(a) still has exact size, and argue that its power against changes in α tends to zero as β1→0. What happens to the Box–Tidwell step, and to the likelihood ratio interval for α?

exr-tr-poisson-scales.title: B2
exr-tr-poisson-scales.html: Let Y be Poisson with a large mean μ. Use the first-order expansion of the delta method to show that Var(log⁡Y)≈1/μ and Var(Y)≈14, and that EY≈μ. (Read log⁡Y given Y>0, since Pr(Y=0)=e−μ.) If 𝛃μ=exp⁡(x⊤β), which scale has a linear mean and which a constant variance?

exr-tr-poisson-variance-limit.title: C2
exr-tr-poisson-variance-limit.html: @cor-tr-classical(a) is a statement about distributions. Show that the variance converges too: 4VarY→1 as μ→∞ for Y∼Poisson(μ). Use the bound (Y−μ)2≤(Y−μ)2/μ, and the fact that a family of nonnegative random variables that converges in distribution, and whose means converge to the mean of the limit, is uniformly integrable.

exr-tr-power-law-ridge.title: B2
exr-tr-power-law-ridge.html: Suppose y=cxβ exactly, with c,β>0. Show that for λ≠0, y(λ) is an affine function of x(α) iff α=βλ, and that for λ=0 it is affine in x(α) iff α=0. Explain why data close to a power law give a joint likelihood for (λ,α) with a ridge, and why the slope of the ridge need not be exactly β when the variance also depends on λ.

exr-tr-r2-scales.title: B3
exr-tr-r2-scales.html: A colleague fits the same regressors to y and to log⁡y and prefers the log model because its R2 is larger. Explain why the two values of R2 are not comparable. Then take x=(0,1,2) and y=(1,8,7), fit a straight line to y and to log⁡y, and compare the two values of R2 with the residual sums of squares on the original scale, using exp of the fitted values for the log model.

exr-tr-removable.title: C1
exr-tr-removable.html: In a 2×2 layout let μij=(ai+bj)2 with positive ai,bj. Show that the interaction contrast μ11−μ12−μ21+μ22 is 2(a1−a2)(b1−b2), and that it is zero on the square-root scale. Now let Yij=μij+εij with independent errors of variance σ2. Is the table of EYij exactly additive? Relate your answer to the caution in Section 16.2.

exr-tr-several-powers.title: C2
exr-tr-several-powers.html: Let 𝛃E(Y)=X3β3+β1x1(α1)+β2x2(α2). Show that one Gauss–Newton step from (α10,α20) and the least squares coefficients there changes αj by γ^j/β^j, where γ^1,γ^2 are the coefficients of the two constructed variables in a single regression of y on the model matrix augmented by both.

exr-tr-shifted.title: B3
exr-tr-shifted.html: For data that may include zeros, consider the shifted family (y+c)(λ) with an unknown c such that every yi+c>0. Write the log-likelihood of 𝛃(β,σ2,λ,c), show that the profile log-likelihood of (λ,c) is @eq-tr-profile with z(λ) computed from yi+c and its geometric mean, and state the likelihood ratio confidence region for (λ,c).

exr-tr-smear-vs-normal.title: A1
exr-tr-smear-vs-normal.html: For Engel’s log–log fit s2=0.01871. Check that exp⁡(s2/2) is 1.0094. The smearing factor is 1.0091. Why are the two so close here, and in what kind of data would they differ substantially?

exr-tr-smearing-general.title: C1
exr-tr-smearing-general.html: Extend @prp-tr-retransformation(c) to a general strictly increasing h that is continuously differentiable with |h′(t)|≤K(1+eκ|t|) for some constants, assuming Eeκ′|ε|<∞ for some κ′>κ. Show that 𝛃n−1∑ih(x0⊤β^+ε^i) converges in probability to E(Y∣x0). (Use the mean value theorem and the bound on maxi|ε^i−εi| from the proof.)

exr-tr-spread-level.title: B3
exr-tr-spread-level.html: Replicate observations at four settings have means 10, 40, 160, 640 and standard deviations 2, 5.7, 16, 45. Fit the spread–level line log⁡s=c+alog⁡μ described above by eye or by least squares, and use @cor-tr-classical(d) to choose the power.

exr-tr-sqrt-smearing.title: B2
exr-tr-sqrt-smearing.html: Let 𝛃Yi=x(i)⊤β+εi with 1∈C(X). Show that 𝛃E(Y∣x0)=(x0⊤β)2+σ2 and that the smearing estimate 𝛃n−1∑i(x0⊤β^+ε^i)2 equals 𝛃(x0⊤β^)2+SSE/n. How does this compare with the plug-in estimate 𝛃(x0⊤β^)2+s2?

exr-tr-tidwell-derivative.title: B1
exr-tr-tidwell-derivative.html: Show that ∂x(α)/∂α=xαlog⁡x/α−x(α)/α for α≠0, and that its limit as α→0 is 12(log⁡x)2. Conclude that in a model containing 1 and x(α0) the constructed variable may be taken to be @eq-tr-power-constructed.

exr-tr-tidwell-hand.title: A1
exr-tr-tidwell-hand.html: At α0=1 a fit gives β^1=2.5, and adding xlog⁡x gives it the coefficient γ^=−1.5. What is the next Box–Tidwell value of α? What does the sign of γ^ say about the curvature of the relation?

exr-tr-why-normalize.title: A2
exr-tr-why-normalize.html: Show that if every yi is multiplied by c>0, the residual sum of squares of the unnormalized y(λ) in a model with an intercept is multiplied by c2λ. Conclude that choosing λ by minimizing the unnormalized residual sum of squares would give an answer that depends on the units of y.

prp-tr-back-intervals.title: Intervals after a transformation
prp-tr-back-intervals.html:
Assume @eq-tr-transformed-model, and let Y0 be a new response at x0, independent of Y and following the same model.

  1. If L≤U are statistics with values in the range of g such that Pr{L≤g(Y0)≤U}=1−α, then Pr{h(L)≤Y0≤h(U)}=1−α. Under normal errors the prediction interval of @thm-ci-prediction-interval therefore transforms into an exact prediction interval for Y0.

  2. If [L,U] is a confidence interval for 𝛃x0⊤β with coverage 1−α and F has median 0, then [h(L),h(U)] is a confidence interval for the median of Y0 with coverage 1−α.

  3. Let g=log, let the errors be normal, and let X have rank r<n with x0∈C(X⊤) and h0=x0⊤(X⊤X)−x0. The logarithm of the mean, 𝛃θ=x0⊤β+σ2/2, is estimated by 𝛃θ^=x0⊤β^+s2/2, which is unbiased with Var(θ^)=σ2h0+σ42(n−r).{#eq-tr-mean-variance}

prp-tr-constructed.title: A constructed variable for the response power
prp-tr-constructed.title_html: A constructed variable for the response power
prp-tr-constructed.html:
Let 𝛆ε^0=(I−M)z(λ0) and w=w(λ0), with w∉C(X).

  1. 𝛆ddλSSEz(λ)|λ0=2ε^0⊤w, and so 𝛆ℓp′(λ0)=−nε^0⊤w/SSEz(λ0).

  2. In the least squares fit of z(λ0) on [X,w], the coefficient of w is 𝛆γ^=ε^0⊤w/‖(I−M)w‖2. Hence γ^ and ℓp′(λ0) have opposite signs, and γ^=0 iff λ0 is a stationary point of the profile log-likelihood. In particular γ^=0 at an interior maximum λ0=λ^.

prp-tr-cpr.title: What the plot shows
prp-tr-cpr.html:
Let X=[x1,X2] have full column rank, with 1∈C(X2), and let 𝛃β^ and 𝛆ε^ be the coefficients and residuals of the least squares fit of y on X. Let M and M2 project onto C(X) and C(X2), and x~1=(I−M2)x1.

  1. If 𝛃E(Y)=g+X2β2, where g has entries g(xi1) for some function g, then 𝛆E(ε^+β^1x1)=g−M2(g−bx1),b=E(β^1)=x~1⊤g‖x~1‖2.{#eq-tr-cpr-mean}

  2. In particular, if C(X2) is spanned by 1 alone, the expected partial residuals are g shifted by a constant, so the plot shows g exactly apart from its level.

prp-tr-elasticity.title: Elasticities in a transformed model
prp-tr-elasticity.html:
Let x1>0, and suppose that the median m(x) of Y satisfies m(x)(λ)=β0+β1x1(α)+c(x−1), where c does not involve x1 and the Box–Cox transformation @eq-tr-box-cox is applied to both m and x1. Then ∂m∂x1=β1x1α−1m1−λ,x1m∂m∂x1=β1x1αm−λ.{#eq-tr-elasticity}

In particular the elasticity is the constant β1 in the log–log model (λ=α=0), β1x1 in the log–level model (λ=0, α=1), β1/m in the level–log model (λ=1, α=0) and β1x1/m in the untransformed model. Under @eq-tr-multiplicative the mean is a constant multiple of the median, so for λ=0 the elasticity of the mean is the same.

prp-tr-family.title: Properties of the family
prp-tr-family.html:
Let y>0.

  1. y(λ)→log⁡y as λ→0, so λ↦y(λ) is continuous.

  2. For each λ, y↦y(λ) is strictly increasing on (0,∞), with derivative yλ−1. The normalized transformation has derivative (y/y˙)λ−1, which equals 1 at y=y˙ for every λ.

  3. If p<q, then y(q)=φ(y(p)) for a strictly increasing and strictly convex function φ. Equivalently, moving down the ladder from q to p applies a strictly concave increasing function.

  4. As y ranges over (0,∞), y(λ) ranges over (−1/λ,∞) if λ>0, over (−∞,−1/λ) if λ<0, and over R if λ=0.

prp-tr-multiplicative.title: Multiplicative errors
prp-tr-multiplicative.html:
Let the model matrix X have first column 1, with β0 the corresponding coefficient, and let 𝛃Yi=exp⁡(x(i)⊤β)Ui,i=1,…,n,{#eq-tr-multiplicative}

where U1,…,Un are independent and identically distributed positive random variables with ν=E(log⁡Ui) and τ2=Var(log⁡Ui) finite.

  1. The logarithms follow the linear model with constant variance: log⁡Yi=(β0+ν)+∑j≥1xijβj+εi, where εi=log⁡Ui−ν are independent with mean 0 and variance τ2. The slopes are β1,…,βp−1, unchanged; only the intercept absorbs ν.

  2. If E(Ui2)<∞, then 𝛃E(Yi)=exp⁡(x(i)⊤β)E(U1) and the standard deviation of Yi is 𝛃exp⁡(x(i)⊤β) times that of U1. The standard deviation is proportional to the mean, so the coefficient of variation is the same for every case.

  3. For two regressor profiles x and x′, every quantile of Y at x′ is 𝛃exp⁡{(x′−x)⊤β} times the same quantile at x. The same ratio holds for the geometric means exp⁡E(log⁡Y), and for the means when they are finite.

prp-tr-retransformation.title: Retransformation bias and the smearing estimate
prp-tr-retransformation.title_html: Retransformation bias and the smearing estimate
prp-tr-retransformation.html:
Assume @eq-tr-transformed-model.

  1. Quantiles. If ξq is a q-quantile of F, then 𝛃h(x⊤β+ξq) is a q-quantile of Y at x. In particular, if F has median 0 (for instance, if it is symmetric), the median of Y at x is 𝛃h(x⊤β).

  2. Means. 𝛃E(Y∣x)=∫h(x⊤β+e)dF(e) whenever this is finite. If h is strictly convex and σ2>0, then 𝛃E(Y∣x)>h(x⊤β). For h=exp, 𝛃E(Y∣x)=exp⁡(x⊤β)Eeε, and for normal errors Eeε=exp⁡(σ2/2).

  3. Smearing. Let h=exp, let X have full column rank p for every n, with leverages hii, and let the εi be the first n terms of an independent and identically distributed sequence with Eeε<∞. If maxihii→0 as n→∞, then the smearing factor satisfies 1n∑i=1nexp⁡(ε^i)→Eeεin probability.{#eq-tr-smearing}

    If moreover 𝛃𝛃x0⊤β^→x0⊤β in probability, the smearing estimate 𝛃exp⁡(x0⊤β^)n−1∑iexp⁡(ε^i) converges in probability to E(Y∣x0).

prp-tr-units.title: Units of the response
prp-tr-units.html: Suppose 1∈C(X). If every yi is multiplied by the same c>0, then SSEz(λ) is multiplied by c2 for every λ. Consequently ℓp changes by a constant, and λ^, the likelihood ratio statistics and the set @eq-tr-lr-interval are unchanged.

thm-tr-box-cox.title: Profile likelihood of the Box–Cox parameter
thm-tr-box-cox.title_html: Profile likelihood of the Box–Cox parameter
thm-tr-box-cox.html:
Let X have rank r<n, let y1,…,yn>0, and for each λ let SSEz(λ)=‖(I−M)z(λ)‖2, assumed positive. Under the model above:

  1. the log-likelihood of 𝛃(β,σ2,λ) is 𝛃𝛃ℓ(β,σ2,λ)=−n2log⁡(2πσ2)−‖y(λ)−Xβ‖22σ2+(λ−1)∑i=1nlog⁡yi;{#eq-tr-box-cox-loglik}

  2. for fixed λ it is maximized by the least squares fit of y(λ) on X, and the profile log-likelihood of λ is ℓp(λ)=−n2{log⁡(2πSSEz(λ)n)+1},{#eq-tr-profile}

    so the maximum likelihood estimate λ^ is the value that minimizes SSEz(λ);

  3. the likelihood ratio statistic for H:λ=λ0 is 2{ℓp(λ^)−ℓp(λ0)}=nlog⁡{SSEz(λ0)/SSEz(λ^)}, and the likelihood ratio confidence set of level 1−α is {λ0: nlog⁡SSEz(λ0)SSEz(λ^)≤χ1,α2},{#eq-tr-lr-interval}

    where χ1,α2 is the upper α point of χ2(1).

thm-tr-box-tidwell.title: Box–Tidwell
thm-tr-box-tidwell.html:
Let X0=[X2,x(α0)] have full column rank p, with 1∈C(X2), let w be the constructed variable @eq-tr-power-constructed, and suppose [X0,w] has full column rank p+1<n. Let β^1 be the coefficient of x(α0) and 𝛆ε^0 the residual vector in the least squares fit of y on X0, and let γ^ be the coefficient of w in the fit of y on [X0,w].

  1. Exact test. If 𝛃Y∼Nn(X0β,σ2I), which is @eq-tr-box-tidwell with α=α0, then the t statistic of γ^ has the t(n−p−1) distribution.

  2. The step. If β^1≠0, one Gauss–Newton step for minimizing 𝛃‖y−X2β2−β1x(α)‖2, started from the least squares coefficients at α0, moves α to α1=α0+γ^/β^1.{#eq-tr-power-step}

  3. Stationarity. SSE(α) is differentiable at α0 with 𝛆SSE′(α0)=−2β^1ε^0⊤w=−2β^1γ^‖(I−M0)w‖2, where M0 projects onto C(X0). So if β^1≠0, then γ^=0 iff α0 is a stationary point of SSE, and every fixed point of the iteration @eq-tr-power-step is a stationary point.

thm-tr-variance-stabilizing.title: Variance-stabilizing transformations
thm-tr-variance-stabilizing.html:
Let I be an open interval and v:I→(0,∞) continuous. Suppose that for every θ∈I the random variables Tm satisfy m(Tm−θ)→N(0,v(θ)) in distribution as m→∞. Fix t0∈I and let g(t)=∫t0tv(s)−1/2ds for t∈I, extended in any way outside I.

  1. For every θ∈I, m{g(Tm)−g(θ)}→N(0,1) in distribution.

  2. If h:I→R is continuously differentiable and m{h(Tm)−h(θ)}→N(0,1) for every θ∈I, then h=g+c or h=−g+c on I for a constant c.
